Tullock Creek would show about a one percent reduction in flow. These figures assume complete drainage control on both Tracts. Ground Water
All aquifers above the base of the Robinson coal will be destroyed in mined areas. The replaced spoil will have different hydrological characteristics than the original rock and may have a tendency to transmit water more rapidly to discharge areas. Hydraulic gradients in the ground-water reservoir adjacent to the mine area will be steepened, and flow paths will change. Existing spring flow from the coals will be affected, perhaps for many years or permanently. Springs currently receiving recharge from the interburden and stratigraphically higher units probably will be lost. Springs currently associated with the Robinson coal will probably receive recharge from the unconsolidated spoil after mining and may exhibit more seasonal flow patterns due to increased permeability. Water supplies below the Robinson coal will not be affected. Pumpage of large quantities of water for dust control will locally lower the head in the Madison Limestone during the life of mining operations.
